brief.notification_title: Tech rout: Nasdaq -3.4%, SMH stop hit, oil firm
brief.market_summary: With about 20 minutes left in Friday's session, AI spending fears are driving a tech selloff. The Nasdaq is down 3.36% at 25,305, SMH is down 8.9% and the S&P 500 is down 2.19% at 7,551. Money is moving into staples, health care, utilities and energy, and VIX has jumped 28% to 21.99. Treasuries are rallying as a safe haven even though Fed officials are openly calling for more hikes: the 10Y is at 4.92% (−6.8bp) and the 5Y at 4.72% (−8bp). Brent is still near its highs after a tanker attack in Hormuz and record quarters from Exxon and Chevron. Crypto is the weakest asset: after Binance's $6.3bn hack, BTC is at $76,361 (−5.5%) and sitting on a widely watched support level.
brief.since_last:
1) Intel's Q4 guidance (revenue $15–16bn vs $17.1bn expected, EPS $0.25 vs $0.43) sank the stock about 31% and dragged semis down. Amazon missed on EPS ($1.89 vs $2.01) but kept its ~$220bn capex plan, and the stock recovered from −7% before the open to about −2%. Investors are now focused on how much cash the AI build-out burns (n19, n2).
2) Exxon (adjusted $4.23) and Chevron (adjusted $5.28) both beat comfortably and hit record highs (n80).
3) Fed officials Logan, Musalem and Barkin all called for more hikes. One preview puts the odds of a December hike near 80% (n25, n33).
4) Binance lost $6.36bn to North Korea-linked hackers. About $3bn is frozen, Binance says it will cover the losses, and it is aiming to restart withdrawals on Sunday (n90).
5) A tanker attack in Hormuz and Houthi claims of strikes on Saudi oil sites pushed December Brent above $117 before it expired (n160).
6) SMH fell through the $530 invalidation level in the last brief, so that idea is closed.

economic_data.when: 08:30 ET (news reports say Thu 29 Oct; the calendar feed says 30 Oct)
economic_data.takeaway: Growth was stronger than expected, which gives the Fed room to resume hiking. The GDP price index was 2.2% vs 3.2% expected, but the monthly PCE data below show inflation is still running hot.
In line. It is the third straight 0.3%, which annualizes to well above 3%. The Fed's hawks have nothing here that argues against hiking.
Core inflation is drifting higher, not lower, which backs Logan's call for at least two more hikes and the roughly 80% odds of a December hike. That is bad for long-duration growth stocks.
Oil is pushing headline inflation up. With Brent above $110, energy keeps feeding into prices and the Fed can't offset a supply shock (n42).

Both missed. Real spending was flat, real incomes fell and the saving rate is at a multiyear low. Consumers are being squeezed, which helps explain why staples and health care are favored over discretionary.
The labor market is still tight; continuing claims are the lowest in more than three years. Nothing here would hold the Fed back.
In line and slightly slower. Pay is rising more slowly than inflation for a second straight quarter (n98), so wages are not driving a spiral. That is a small dovish offset.
I couldn't find the actual print, so I can't use it.
Demand was solid on a safe-haven day, and the yield was about 19bp below last month's. That supports the 5–10Y rally.
Crude and diesel stocks fell more than expected, which fits the strong refining margins in the Exxon and Chevron results. The gasoline build is a small bearish offset.
A strong print would add to December hike odds and pressure tech again. A miss would extend the bond rally.

The deciding data point for a December hike. A weak number with soft wages would be the Fed's first reason to pause, which helps duration and tech. A strong one locks in the hike.

sections.summary: Tech led the market lower on a second day of AI disappointment (Alphabet −12.6% on Thursday, Intel −31% today). The Nasdaq is headed for its worst day since June, and the Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 together have shed about $3.3tn (n2). The rest of the market held up better: staples, health care, utilities and energy are all up, and the Dow is still on track for about +2.8% in October.

Gainers: XLP +1.41%, XLE +1.54%, XLU +0.68%, XLV +0.36%; REGN +12%, MDLZ +6.8%, AZN +4.5%

sections.summary: Treasuries rallied as a safe haven: 5Y −8bp to 4.72%, 10Y −6.8bp to 4.92%, 30Y only −2.4bp. The curve steepened from the belly out. The rally came despite three Fed officials calling for more hikes, so it is risk-off buying, not a dovish repricing. Credit barely moved (LQD −0.03%, HYG −0.19%), so this is a stock-valuation shock, not a funding or credit event.

sections.summary: December Brent traded above $117 intraday after a tanker was hit by explosives in Hormuz and the Houthis claimed strikes on Ras Tanura, Rabigh and Abqaiq. December expires today, and the snapshot's $113.18 (−1.5%) mostly reflects the switch to the cheaper January contract. BNO (+1.19%) and WTI (+2.2%) show the real move was up. Brent is up about 11% in October, its fourth straight monthly gain.
key_points: Brent is about $3–5 below its wartime closing high of $118.35. The ~$4 December-to-January gap is a contract-roll effect, not selling
Hormuz crude exports fell to 7.3m bpd in the latest week, more than 40% below the prewar level (Kpler, via CNBC). Tankers are still running the strait for very high freight rates (n29)

Downside risks: Vance's letter seeking to restart talks (unanswered for now), the World Bank's $79 forecast for 2027 (n74), and political pressure on oil prices before the midterms

brief.instructor_take: Today is not a recession scare. It is the market repricing what the AI build-out earns. Alphabet's −$9.1bn free cash flow, Amazon's −$42.4bn trailing free cash flow against a reaffirmed $220bn capex budget, and Intel's guidance cut all point the same way: investors no longer pay for spending, they want to see returns. The tell is what didn't break. Credit barely moved, staples and health care rose, and the Dow is still up about 2.8% for October. Money is rotating, not leaving equities. What I think the crowd is missing is the idea that falling tech will make the Fed back off (n149). With core PCE at 3.1% and rising, Brent above $110 and claims at 194K, Logan, Musalem and Barkin are telling you there is no rescue coming before payrolls next Friday. So I'd respect stops on growth exposure, keep the defensive and real-asset tilts that are working, and hold more cash into a binary week: midterms, AMD, refunding, the BoE and payrolls. In crypto I'm staying out until Binance's withdrawals restart and we see what the hacker does with the stolen coins. Buying before that is guessing on an event that could easily go wrong. I'm wrong if AMD and Apple reassure next week and SMH gets back above $530. In that case the AI selloff was a two-day flush, and I'll have given up a bounce in exchange for having stayed safe.

top_ideas.title: Exit SMH: the $530 stop has broken
top_ideas.one_liner: SMH broke the $530 stop: exit and park the cash in SGOV
top_ideas.thesis: SMH is at $511.76, well below the $530 close that invalidated the last brief's idea, after Intel's guidance cut and the market turning against AI cash burn. Sell the one-third tranche and move the cash to SGOV (13-week bills about 3.97%) until AMD reports.
top_ideas.reasoning: I set $530 as the line where the case stops working, and SMH is 3.5% below it with minutes left in the session. Breaking that level means the thesis is wrong for now. One part of the case did hold: Amazon reaffirmed its ~$220bn capex and Sandisk beat ($48.92 vs $46.19). But the market has changed what it rewards. Intel beat on EPS and still fell 31% on guidance, and the selloff spread to AMD and Nvidia, which tells me investors are punishing the whole AI supply chain, not just weak companies. The newer investor's mistake is to wait for a bounce to 'get back to even'. That turns a planned 8–9% loss on one-third of a position into an open-ended one, with the Fed leaning toward a hike and payrolls ahead. I choose SGOV over IEF for the cash because I want no duration risk ahead of Wednesday's refunding announcement and a likely December hike, and short bills reset higher if the Fed hikes. I'll look at semis again only if AMD (Tue 3 Nov) reassures on AI demand and SMH closes back above $530. Re-entering higher is a fair price for skipping a possible further 10–15% drop.

top_ideas.title: Health care: hold half, add the rest on a dip
top_ideas.one_liner: XLV $184.71: hold half; add near $180–181 or once ABBV is confirmed
top_ideas.thesis: Big pharma keeps beating and raising (LLY, MRK, GILD, BMY, REGN), and health care is the main beneficiary of the rotation out of tech. The first half bought at $181–184 is working; the second half should be added on a dip, not chased after an 11% monthly gain.
top_ideas.reasoning: The idea rests on earnings revisions: when large companies beat by 12–39% and raise guidance, analysts lift their estimates, and that lifts the sector. Lilly ($7.48 vs $5.38, guide raised to $91–92bn), Merck, Gilead and BMY did that this week, and Regeneron, AstraZeneca and Sanofi all rose on Friday's reports. XLV gained 0.36% on a day the Nasdaq fell 3.4%. It is acting as a defensive with earnings growth, and in this environment, with the Fed hiking and oil above $110, that combination is scarce. I prefer XLV to buying Lilly alone because it spreads single-drug and pricing risk across the sector. The less obvious point is that XLV is up 11% in a month, so the easy money has been made. That is why I'd add on a pullback toward $180–181 rather than at $185. I don't have AbbVie's actual numbers in my material, so check that it beat before the Monday add. A close below $176, or a bounce in tech that pulls money back out of defensives, would tell me the rotation is over.

top_ideas.title: XLE: XOM/CVX confirmed, add one more quarter
top_ideas.one_liner: XOM, CVX beat; Brent ~$113: add a quarter to XLE, keep a quarter for a dip
top_ideas.thesis: Both supermajors beat clearly (XOM adjusted $4.23, CVX adjusted $5.28) on refining and diesel margins, and January Brent is about $112–113, far above the $105 condition. Add one more quarter now and keep the last quarter for a pullback, because the main risk is a ceasefire headline.
top_ideas.reasoning: Last brief I said I'd add once both supermajors confirmed with Brent at $105 or higher. Both are true: Exxon earned $4.23 adjusted against estimates of $3.83–4.08, and Chevron $5.28 against $4.78. Margins on refining crude into diesel are where most of the profit came from. That matters because those profits hold up even if crude itself eases a bit. Supply is the key: Hormuz exports fell more than 40% below the prewar level in the latest week, and attacks are escalating. I buy XLE rather than BNO because the stocks earn on both crude prices and refining margins, they don't suffer from futures-roll costs, and they act as a hedge against the same inflation that is hurting my tech exposure. What I can't confirm is buyback guidance, which isn't in my material, and XLE is near its highs rather than the $67 I wanted. So I'm adding a quarter, not the whole half. A signed US–Iran or Hormuz agreement is the single event that ends this trade: Brent could quickly fall $15–20 and the World Bank already sees $79 in 2027.

lesson.concept: Guidance matters more than the beat
lesson.explanation: Stock prices reflect expected future profits, so a company's outlook for next quarter usually moves the shares more than whether it beat last quarter's estimate. A beat on the past that comes with weaker guidance means estimates for the future fall, and the price follows those estimates. A miss that comes with a reassuring outlook is often forgiven. When you read an earnings report, look at the guidance against consensus before the headline EPS.
lesson.todays_example: Intel beat on EPS ($0.41 vs $0.28 on the calendar feed) and still fell about 31%, because it guided Q4 revenue to $15–16bn vs $17.1bn expected and EPS to $0.25 vs $0.43. Amazon missed on EPS ($1.89 vs $2.01) but kept its capex plan and gave a Q4 sales guide of $240–247bn. It went from −7% before the open to about −2%.
